<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases (CON on incapacitation/coverage, PRO on physics/self-enforcing prevention), and both followed the Q/A format correctly. The decisive swing came in Rebuttal 2, when CON caught PRO's own "cheap, fast" layer (automated speed cameras) as itself being a penalty/enforcement mechanism, exposing that PRO's practical, scalable answer to "what protects the unrebuilt street tonight" was borrowed from the penalty side of the ledger. PRO's closing tried to wall this off by distinguishing "harsher post-crash penalties" from "low-severity automatic camera fines," but that distinction arrived late and never squarely resolved the tension CON had exposed: PRO's fastest, most citywide-scalable tool was consequence-based, not geometric. CON also more directly answered the "cancels out" pressure question by pointing out penalty infrastructure (courts, DMV, patrol) is a sunk asset needing only statutory change, versus redesign needing new physical construction per block — a comparison PRO never fully neutralized beyond asserting paint/humps/cameras can scale as fast, which remained more asserted than demonstrated. PRO's strongest uncontested point — that prevention protects the first, uncaught victim regardless of driver state — stayed live throughout, but CON's coverage/scale argument and the camera-concession trap did more net damage to the opposing case than PRO's rebuttals did to CON's.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 catch that PRO's own fastest "prevention" layer (automated speed cameras) is functionally a penalty/enforcement mechanism, forcing PRO into an unresolved dilemma between conceding the point or losing its fast, scalable coverage claim.</best_rebuttal>
